sources.title: Why Are Icy Surfaces Slippery?
notes: Pressure melting explains slipperiness only in a narrow temperature range.
Ice can develop a premelted, liquid-like surface layer below the bulk melting point.
Recent simulations suggest contact can rearrange surface molecules; researchers say the mechanism is not fully settled.
sources.apa: University of Pennsylvania Almanac. (2026). Why Are Icy Surfaces Slippery?. https://almanac.upenn.edu/articles/why-are-icy-surfaces-slippery

sources.title: Molecular Insight into the Slipperiness of Ice
sources.publisher: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters / PubMed
sources.reliability: Peer-reviewed research indexed by the U.S. National Library of Medicine
notes: Measurements and simulations linked low friction to mobile molecules at the ice surface.
Surface mobility rises with temperature and helps explain why friction changes across cold conditions.
The precise contribution of surface water and other mechanisms remains an active research question.
sources.apa: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters / PubMed. (2018). Molecular Insight into the Slipperiness of Ice. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29741089/
sources.citation: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters / PubMed, 2018

sources.title: Friction on Ice: How Temperature, Pressure, and Speed Control the Slipperiness of Ice
notes: Experiments examined ice friction across temperature, contact pressure and sliding speed.
High local pressure can suppress surface mobility and increase friction.
Near melting, deformation and friction depend on surface geometry and speed.
sources.apa: Physical Review X. (2021). Friction on Ice: How Temperature, Pressure, and Speed Control the Slipperiness of Ice. https://journals.aps.org/prx/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevX.11.011025

sources.title: Why is ice slippery?
sources.publisher: West Texas A&M University, Science Questions with Surprising Answers
notes: Surface molecules have fewer neighbours than molecules in the bulk crystal.
A liquid-like surface layer can exist even when the ice is not visibly melting.
Pressure and friction alone cannot explain slipperiness under every condition.
sources.apa: West Texas A&M University, Science Questions with Surprising Answers. (2013). Why is ice slippery?. https://www.wtamu.edu/~cbaird/sq/2013/12/10/why-is-ice-slippery/
sources.citation: West Texas A&M University, Science Questions with Surprising Answers, 2013

sources.title: Rubber-ice friction
notes: Rubber-on-ice friction depends on temperature and sliding speed.
At some conditions a thin premelted film contributes, while rubber deformation and ice particles also matter.
Results from steel, rubber and skate contacts should not be treated as interchangeable.
